prompts.title: RFP requirement extraction
prompts.prompt:
Here is the full text of an RFP/bid package: [PASTE RFP TEXT]

Extract every requirement, deadline, and submission rule into a numbered
checklist, organized under these headings: Submission Deadlines,
Required Documents/Forms, Rate/Pricing Format Requirements, Insurance
and Compliance Requirements, Service-Level Requirements, and Anything
Unusual or Easy to Miss. Quote the exact source sentence next to each
item so I can verify it against the original.
prompts.note: run this before you write a word of response, and manually skim the RFP once yourself afterward — the "quote the source sentence" instruction is your check; if a line has no quote, don't trust it.

prompts.title: Scope-gap hunt
prompts.prompt:
Here is an RFP scope of work: [PASTE SCOPE SECTION]

Here is a list of services my company currently offers: [LIST YOUR
SERVICES/CAPABILITIES]

Compare the two. List every requirement in the scope that I do not
clearly cover today, every requirement that's ambiguous about whether
I cover it, and every requirement where the RFP's terminology doesn't
match mine (so I know it's the same requirement, worded differently).
prompts.note: this catches the "wrong scope vocabulary" trap from Chapter 4 — read every "ambiguous" item yourself before deciding to bid or pass.

prompts.title: This-year-vs-last-year contract comparison
prompts.prompt:
Here is last year's contract/rate agreement: [PASTE OR SUMMARIZE OLD
TERMS]

Here is this year's RFP or renewal terms: [PASTE NEW TERMS]

List every change: rate changes, new requirements, removed
requirements, changed service levels, changed penalty/chargeback
language. Flag anything that shifts risk or cost onto me that wasn't
there before.
prompts.note: verification reminder — recompute any rate or penalty change by hand; don't take the tool's percentage math on faith.

prompts.title: Cost sensitivity table builder
prompts.prompt:
My stop economics: average revenue per stop is $[X], average cost per
stop is $[Y], broken down as: fuel $[X], labor $[X], vehicle $[X],
overhead allocation $[X]. This RFP proposes a rate of $[PROPOSED RATE]
per stop with estimated volume of [VOLUME] stops per month.

Build a sensitivity table showing my margin per stop and monthly profit
at proposed volume, and at 20% below and 20% above proposed volume.
Also show the breakeven stop count at the proposed rate.
prompts.note: this is arithmetic, not judgment — recompute at least one row by hand before you trust the table, per the Chapter 3 rule.

prompts.title: Accessorial and rate-table sanity check
prompts.prompt:
Here is the accessorial and rate table from an RFP or contract:
[PASTE TABLE]

Check the math: do line items add up the way the total implies? Are
any accessorials priced inconsistently with each other (e.g., a
"long carry" fee lower than a "flight of stairs" fee when my
experience says the reverse should be true)? List anything that looks
like an error or a trap.
prompts.note: flags what to double-check by hand — this tool does not know your actual costs, only whether the numbers in front of it are internally consistent.

prompts.title: Bid boilerplate structure draft
prompts.prompt:
I'm responding to an RFP with these requirements: [PASTE OR SUMMARIZE
KEY REQUIREMENTS]

Draft the standard sections of my bid response — company overview,
compliance certifications list, standard service description, standard
insurance/safety statement — using this information about my company:
[PASTE YOUR BOILERPLATE FACTS: years in business, fleet size, safety
record, certifications]. Keep it factual and specific, no generic
claims without a number behind them.
prompts.note: this is the "below the waterline" work — this draft is scaffolding; you still write the three paragraphs that actually win (local knowledge, named references, specific capability) yourself.

prompts.title: Win-the-bid paragraph sharpener
prompts.prompt:
Here's my draft paragraph making the case for why we're the right
carrier for this lane/region: [PASTE YOUR DRAFT]

Tighten it. Cut every adjective that isn't backed by a fact or number.
Flag any sentence that could be copy-pasted into any other company's
bid without changes — those are the sentences that lose bids.
prompts.note: this is a red-team pass on your own writing, not a rewrite to trust blindly — keep your own voice, use the flags as a to-do list.

prompts.title: Rate benchmarking data organizer
prompts.prompt:
Here is my own historical rate and cost data across lanes/customers:
[PASTE OR DESCRIBE YOUR DATA]

Organize this into a table showing rate per stop, cost per stop, and
margin by lane/customer, sorted from highest to lowest margin. Flag
any lane where the data looks incomplete or inconsistent.
prompts.note: this structures what you already know — it cannot tell you the market rate for a lane it's never seen, only make your own numbers legible to you.

prompts.title: Capability one-pager draft
prompts.prompt:
Write a one-page capability summary for my company for use with
[potential customer type, e.g., regional 3PL / retail DC / property
management company]. Facts to include: [SERVICES, FLEET SIZE, COVERAGE
AREA, YEARS IN BUSINESS, CERTIFICATIONS, NOTABLE CUSTOMERS IF
DISCLOSABLE]. Every claim needs a number attached — no adjectives
without evidence. Keep it to one page.
prompts.note: strip any claim you can't back up with a real number before this leaves your hands — the "every claim gets a number" rule is the whole point.

prompts.title: Cold outreach research brief
prompts.prompt:
I want to find delivery/logistics decision-makers at [TYPE OF COMPANY,
e.g., regional furniture retailers, 3PLs with last-mile programs] in
[REGION]. Help me build a research checklist: what job titles to look
for, what public information (site, LinkedIn, local news) would tell
me they're a fit, and what questions I should be able to answer about
a company before I email them.
prompts.note: this is a research checklist, not a contact list — the tool can't browse and verify current company details for you; you still do the actual lookup.

prompts.title: Cold email that doesn't read like a robot
prompts.prompt:
Draft a short cold email to [TITLE/ROLE] at a [TYPE OF COMPANY] I want
to become a delivery partner for. Facts about my company: [KEY FACTS].
What I know about them: [SPECIFIC DETAIL — a recent expansion, a
facility they run, a problem I can solve]. Keep it under 120 words,
one clear ask, no generic flattery, sound like a person who runs
trucks wrote it.
prompts.note: if it doesn't mention the specific detail you gave it prominently, tell it to lead with that — generic-sounding cold email is exactly what gets deleted.

prompts.title: Weekly content post from a job-site photo
prompts.prompt:
I took a photo today of [DESCRIBE WHAT'S IN THE PHOTO AND WHAT
HAPPENED, e.g., "crew navigating a tight stairwell delivery, took an
extra 20 minutes but got it done clean"]. Write a short, honest social
post (LinkedIn-style, under 150 words) about this real operational
moment — no forced enthusiasm, no hashtag spam, just what happened and
why it mattered.
prompts.note: check it doesn't overstate the story — one honest post a week beats five inflated ones, per Chapter 5.

prompts.title: Website "what we do" page draft
prompts.prompt:
Write the main services page for my company website. My services:
[LIST]. My coverage area: [AREA]. What makes us different from a
generic carrier: [YOUR ANSWER]. Write it in plain language a buyer
skimming on their phone would understand in 20 seconds, not marketing
copy.
prompts.note: read it out loud before publishing — if it sounds like every other trucking website, tell the tool what's actually different about you and try again.

prompts.title: Core message template builder
prompts.prompt:
Here are 10-15 examples of messages I've actually sent customers for
[SCENARIO, e.g., delivery confirmations / ETA updates / reschedule
requests]: [PASTE EXAMPLES OR DESCRIBE THE TYPICAL SITUATION AND WHAT
I USUALLY SAY].

Draft a clean, reusable template for this scenario, with bracketed
placeholders for the details that change each time (date, name, item,
reason). Keep my tone — direct and plain, not corporate.
prompts.note: run this once per template category (aim for the 12 from Chapter 6), then hand-edit each result into your actual voice before saving it as your standard.

prompts.title: Reschedule/exception message draft
prompts.prompt:
A delivery needs to be rescheduled because [REASON]. The customer's
original appointment was [DATE/TIME]. Draft a short message explaining
the change, apologizing appropriately without over-apologizing, and
offering the next available option: [OPTIONS]. Keep it under 80 words.
prompts.note: check the reason and offered options are accurate before sending — a wrong date in a reschedule message creates a second problem on top of the first.

prompts.title: Complaint de-escalation draft
prompts.prompt:
A customer sent this complaint: [PASTE CUSTOMER MESSAGE]

Here's what actually happened, as best I know it: [YOUR VERSION OF
EVENTS]

Draft a calm, professional response that acknowledges their frustration,
states the facts without being defensive, and proposes a next step.
Do not admit fault or offer compensation — flag clearly if you think
this situation needs those and I'll decide.
prompts.note: this is customer-facing and Money-and-Safety-Rule territory — a human reads every word and sends it manually, always; never auto-send a complaint response.

prompts.title: Online review response draft
prompts.prompt:
Here is a customer review: [PASTE REVIEW]

Draft a public response. If it's positive, keep it short and specific
(thank them for something concrete in their review, not generic).
If it's negative, stay professional, don't relitigate the complaint
publicly, and invite them to contact us directly to resolve it.
prompts.note: verify any specific claim the reviewer makes against your own records before your response references it — don't confirm a detail you haven't checked.

prompts.title: FAQ auto-answer script
prompts.prompt:
Here are the 10 questions customers ask most often: [LIST QUESTIONS].
Here are the correct answers for my business: [LIST ANSWERS].

Write short, friendly, accurate responses for each, suitable for a
chat widget or auto-reply. Keep each answer under 40 words. Flag any
question where the answer depends on order-specific details that can't
be automated.
prompts.note: only deploy the flagged-safe answers to automation; anything order-specific or money-related routes to a human, per Chapter 6.

prompts.title: Document field extraction (BOL/POD/rate confirmation)
prompts.prompt:
Here is a photo/scan of a [BOL / POD / rate confirmation / invoice]:
[PASTE TEXT OR DESCRIBE ATTACHED IMAGE]

Extract the following into a clean list: date, reference/PO number,
origin, destination, item description, quantity, rate/amount, and any
signature or exception notes. If any field is unreadable or missing,
say so explicitly instead of guessing.
prompts.note: the "say so explicitly instead of guessing" instruction is doing the real work here — spot-check a sample of extractions against the source per the Chapter 7 protocol before you trust the pipeline.

prompts.title: Invoice three-way match
prompts.prompt:
Here is what was contracted: [PASTE RATE/CONTRACT TERMS]
Here is what was delivered/completed: [PASTE DELIVERY/POD DATA]
Here is what was invoiced: [PASTE INVOICE DATA]

Compare all three. List every line item where they don't match —
quantity, rate, or accessorial discrepancies — and calculate the
dollar difference for each.
prompts.note: recompute every flagged dollar difference by hand before you dispute or pay an invoice — this feeds a real payment decision, so it's Money-and-Safety territory.

prompts.title: Messy notes to structured spreadsheet row
prompts.prompt:
Here are my rough notes from today's deliveries: [PASTE NOTES]

Turn this into rows for a spreadsheet with these columns: Date,
Customer, Address, Status (Delivered/Exception/Rescheduled), Notes.
One row per stop.
prompts.note: scan the output against your notes once before importing — this is high-volume, low-risk work, but a misread name or address still needs catching.

prompts.title: Batch document summary
prompts.prompt:
Here are the contents of [NUMBER] documents: [PASTE OR LIST]

Summarize each in one line: document type, key dates, key dollar
amounts, and anything that needs my attention (missing signature,
unusual terms, expired date).
prompts.note: use this to triage a stack fast, then open the flagged ones individually — don't treat the one-line summary as the final read on anything with a dollar amount attached.

prompts.title: Morning exception triage
prompts.prompt:
Here are last night's emails, texts, and voicemail transcripts:
[PASTE OR SUMMARIZE OVERNIGHT MESSAGES]

Turn this into a ranked list of today's problems: what needs a call
in the next 30 minutes, what needs a decision today, and what can wait.
For each item, give me one line on what happened and who's involved.
prompts.note: this replaces the first ten minutes of triage, not your judgment on ranking — re-order anything that doesn't match your gut on urgency; you know the customer relationships the tool doesn't.

prompts.title: Load/cube sanity check
prompts.prompt:
Here's today's load list: [PASTE ITEMS WITH DIMENSIONS/WEIGHTS] and
truck capacity: [CAPACITY]. Flag anything that looks like it won't fit
by weight or cube, and flag any sequencing issue (heavy items loaded
in a way that blocks earlier stops).
prompts.note: this is a second-check, not a load plan — your dispatcher's read still governs; use this to catch what got missed in a rushed morning.

prompts.title: Coverage scramble comms draft
prompts.prompt:
[DRIVER/CREW] is out today and I need to notify affected customers.
Here's the stop list affected: [LIST]. Draft a short notification
message for each, explaining a schedule adjustment without oversharing
internal details, and a short internal message to whoever's covering
with the key details they need.
prompts.note: verify the new schedule times are actually confirmed before these go out — don't let a draft become a promise you can't keep.

prompts.title: Monthly exception pattern review
prompts.prompt:
Here is a list of this month's exceptions/delays/claims: [PASTE DATA:
date, customer, crew, product type, root cause if known]

Summarize patterns: which crews, customers, product types, or stop
types show up most often. Group root causes into categories. Suggest
what's worth investigating further.
prompts.note: treat the groupings as a starting hypothesis, not a verdict — small sample sizes can make noise look like a pattern; check counts before you act on any one crew or customer.

prompts.title: Claims packet assembly
prompts.prompt:
Here are my notes and evidence on an incident: [PASTE NOTES, PHOTOS
DESCRIPTIONS, TIMELINE OF EVENTS]. Here is the relevant contract
language on liability/claims: [PASTE CONTRACT SECTION]

Assemble a claims packet with these sections: Timeline of Events,
Evidence List (what exists and where), Relevant Contract Citations,
and Summary of Position. Flag any gap in evidence or timeline that
would weaken the packet.
prompts.note: verify every date, dollar figure, and quoted contract clause against the source file before this packet goes anywhere — a hallucinated date in a claims letter is a lost claim, per Chapter 9.

prompts.title: Dispute letter / denial rebuttal draft
prompts.prompt:
Here is a claim denial or dispute I received: [PASTE THE DENIAL/
DISPUTE LETTER]. Here are the facts as I know them: [YOUR VERSION,
WITH EVIDENCE]. Here's the relevant contract language: [PASTE]

Draft a firm, professional rebuttal letter that addresses their stated
reasons point by point and cites the contract language and evidence
supporting my position.
prompts.note: this drafts the argument; you verify every citation and fact against the actual file before it goes out, and it does not go to an insurer or attorney's desk without their review first if the situation calls for it.

prompts.title: Customer damage correspondence
prompts.prompt:
A customer's property was damaged during delivery. Here's what
happened: [FACTS]. Draft a message to the customer explaining next
steps in our claims process, professional and empathetic, without
admitting fault or offering a settlement amount.
prompts.note: hard line from Chapter 9 — no admission of fault, no settlement number, ever, drafted by AI or otherwise, without your explicit sign-off and, where warranted, your insurer's.

prompts.title: Quarterly claims pattern report
prompts.prompt:
Here is a full year (or quarter) of claims data: [PASTE: date, crew,
product type, retailer/customer, root cause, dollar amount]

Analyze by crew, product type, and root cause. Show which categories
account for the most dollar exposure and the most frequency separately
— they're often not the same category. Summarize in a short report I
can use for a team conversation.
prompts.note: recheck the dollar totals against your own records before presenting this to anyone — it's directly feeding decisions about crews and cost.

prompts.title: Job post that attracts real crew
prompts.prompt:
I need to hire a [ROLE, e.g., delivery driver / helper / dispatcher]
for my [TYPE OF BUSINESS]. Key requirements: [LIST]. Pay range: [RANGE].
What makes working here different: [YOUR ANSWER]. Write a job post in
plain language, no corporate-speak, that would make someone who
actually does this work want to apply.
prompts.note: check pay range and requirements are accurate and legally compliant for your state/city before posting — the tool doesn't know your local wage or classification rules.

prompts.title: Screening question set
prompts.prompt:
I'm hiring a [ROLE]. The most common ways this job goes wrong are:
[LIST FAILURE MODES, e.g., no-shows, careless handling, poor customer
manner]. Draft 8-10 structured interview questions that would help me
spot these risks in a 30-minute interview, plus what a strong vs. weak
answer sounds like for each.
prompts.note: have someone check the questions for anything that edges into protected-category territory (age, family status, disability) before using them — the tool drafts, you and your judgment decide who's hired, never the AI.

prompts.title: New-hire onboarding sequence
prompts.prompt:
Here's what a new [ROLE] needs to know in their first two weeks:
[LIST TOPICS: safety, equipment, routes, customer interaction
standards, paperwork]. Build a day-by-day onboarding checklist for the
first two weeks, with what to cover each day and what "ready to work
solo" looks like.
prompts.note: walk through it with an actual new hire once and adjust — a checklist built from your head always misses something obvious until it's tested.

prompts.title: SOP from dictation
prompts.prompt:
Here's a rough voice-to-text transcript of me explaining how we handle
[TASK, e.g., a stairwell delivery that won't fit]: [PASTE TRANSCRIPT]

Turn this into a clean one-page SOP: numbered steps, a short checklist
at the end, and a "when to call for help" section. Keep my terminology,
don't add steps I didn't describe.
prompts.note: hand it to the newest crew member and watch where they stumble — that's your real verification step, not a read-through at your desk.

prompts.title: Bookkeeping categorization assist
prompts.prompt:
Here is a list of transactions with descriptions and amounts:
[PASTE TRANSACTION LIST]. Here are my standard expense categories:
[LIST CATEGORIES]

Suggest a category for each transaction and flag any that are
ambiguous or that you're not confident about.
prompts.note: a human or your bookkeeper reviews and approves every categorization before it's final — AI assists the books, it does not close them, per Chapter 10.

prompts.title: Monthly cash-flow narrative
prompts.prompt:
Here is this month's cash-flow summary compared to last month:
[PASTE NUMBERS: revenue, major expense categories, ending cash
position]

Write a short plain-English narrative explaining what changed and
likely why, based on the categories that moved most. Flag anything
that looks like it needs a closer look.
prompts.note: this explains movement, it doesn't audit accuracy — reconcile the underlying numbers with your bookkeeper or accountant before treating the narrative as fact.

prompts.title: Expense summary for the accountant
prompts.prompt:
Here are this month's receipts/transactions: [PASTE OR LIST]

Organize into a summary by category with subtotals, flag anything
that looks miscategorized or duplicated, and format it the way my
accountant would want to receive it: [DESCRIBE FORMAT IF KNOWN].
prompts.note: this is a draft-everything-for-the-accountant step — your accountant still reviews and files; this just saves them (and you) the sorting time.

prompts.title: Quote-intake extraction
prompts.prompt:
Here is an inbound quote request email: [PASTE EMAIL]

Extract: customer name, contact info, origin, destination, item(s)
and quantity, requested timeline, and any special requirements. If any
field is missing, list it as "not provided" rather than guessing.
prompts.note: this is the first step of the Chapter 11 quote-intake automation — the draft quote it feeds into still lands in your drafts folder for a human to check and send, never auto-sent.

prompts.title: Draft quote from extracted details
prompts.prompt:
Here are the extracted details of a quote request: [PASTE EXTRACTED
FIELDS]. Here are my standard rate rules: [PASTE YOUR RATE LOGIC/
RANGES]. 

Draft a quote response email using these rules, showing the rate
breakdown clearly. If the request falls outside my standard rate
rules, flag it instead of guessing a number.
prompts.note: recompute the quoted number yourself before it goes out — this drafts price, and price is Money-and-Safety territory, no exceptions.

prompts.title: Automation scope brief for a freelancer
prompts.prompt:
I want to automate this workflow: [DESCRIBE THE WORKFLOW STEP BY STEP,
TRIGGER TO OUTCOME]. Write a clear project brief for a freelancer or
automation builder: what triggers it, what data is involved, what the
output should look like, what "done" means, and what should never
happen without my review.
prompts.note: use this brief to get comparable quotes from more than one builder — if a quote is wildly higher or promises far more than the brief describes, that's the red flag from Chapter 11.

prompts.title: Automation break diagnosis
prompts.prompt:
This automation stopped working correctly: [DESCRIBE WHAT IT'S SUPPOSED
TO DO AND WHAT'S GOING WRONG]. Here's a sample of the input that's
failing: [PASTE EXAMPLE]. What are the most likely reasons an
automation like this would break, given this input?
prompts.note: this is a first-pass diagnostic to bring to whoever built or maintains the automation, not a guaranteed fix — treat it as a hypothesis list for your monthly 15-minute check.

prompts.title: 30-day workflow tracker setup
prompts.prompt:
I'm rolling out this AI workflow starting this week: [DESCRIBE
WORKFLOW]. Help me design a simple tracking sheet: what to measure
(hours saved, error rate, response time — pick what's relevant), how
often to log it, and what a "keep" vs. "kill" threshold should look
like after 30 days.
prompts.note: fill in real numbers weekly, don't skip a week because it felt fine — the whole point is a number at the end, not a feeling.

prompts.title: Keep/kill decision summary
prompts.prompt:
Here's 30 days of data on a workflow I tested: [PASTE YOUR NUMBERS:
hours before/after, error count, any other metric you tracked]

Summarize whether this workflow is worth keeping, and why, in three
sentences I could say out loud to my team.
prompts.note: this organizes your own data into a decision — the decision itself, and the discipline to actually kill something that isn't working, is yours.

prompts.title: "What did you assume?" follow-up
prompts.prompt:
Before I use that, list every assumption you made in producing this
answer, and flag anything you weren't given that you'd normally need
to know to get this right.
prompts.note: run this after any prompt that touches a number, a date, or a decision — it's the single cheapest verification habit in the book (Chapter 3), and it works as a follow-up to any prompt above.

prompts.title: Plain-English explainer
prompts.prompt:
Explain [TOPIC/DOCUMENT/CLAUSE] to me the way you'd explain it to a
business owner with no legal or technical background. No jargon. If
a term is unavoidable, define it in the same sentence.
prompts.note: useful anywhere a contract, a piece of software documentation, or a technical explanation is slowing you down — always cross-check anything that changes a decision against the original source.

prompts.title: Shorten-and-tighten pass
prompts.prompt:
Here's a draft I wrote: [PASTE YOUR DRAFT]

Cut it by [PERCENTAGE OR WORD COUNT] without losing the key facts.
Keep my voice — don't make it sound more formal or more corporate.
prompts.note: read the shortened version for meaning, not just length — a tightening pass occasionally drops something you needed; that's on you to catch.

prompts.title: Meeting/call notes to action list
prompts.prompt:
Here are my rough notes from a call/meeting: [PASTE NOTES]

Turn this into a short action list: what needs to happen, who owns
it, and any deadline mentioned. Flag anything unclear that I should
confirm with the other party.
prompts.note: confirm anything flagged as unclear before you act on it — don't let the tool's best guess replace an actual follow-up question.

prompts.title: Contract clause risk scan
prompts.prompt:
Here is a contract or clause: [PASTE TEXT]

In plain English, explain what this clause requires of me, what
happens if I don't meet it, and flag anything that looks unusual
compared to standard industry terms.
prompts.note: this is a first read, not a legal opinion — anything flagged as unusual, or any clause with real dollar exposure, goes to an actual attorney before you sign, per the Money-and-Safety Rule.

prompts.title: Vendor/quote comparison table
prompts.prompt:
Here are quotes/proposals from [NUMBER] vendors for [WHAT YOU'RE
BUYING]: [PASTE OR SUMMARIZE EACH]

Build a comparison table: price, what's included, what's excluded,
timeline, and anything that looks like a red flag (vague scope,
unusually low price, missing details).
prompts.note: works for anything from insurance quotes to the automation-builder scoping in Chapter 11 — verify the "included/excluded" column against the actual quote documents, don't take the summary as final.

prompts.title: Daily ops digest
prompts.prompt:
Here's everything that came in today across email, texts, and any
system notifications: [PASTE OR SUMMARIZE]

Give me a five-line digest: what needs action today, what's FYI only,
and what's building into a pattern worth watching (repeat customer,
repeat issue, repeat crew).
prompts.note: this is the Chapter 11 daily-digest automation in prompt form — start by running it manually for a week before you wire it into an automated pipeline, so you know what "good" looks like.
